items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: there were great banjo players and guitar players come out of Baltimore. Banjo Bernie. Him, Bernard Addison. Aw man, so many I recall.

ctx.x: But, did you play . . . if you played the C chord, the C was on top, and then the E and G, whatever?

According to the arranger, what he has there. The sound of the arrangement. They had a hell of arrangers in them days, like Andy Gibson. Who else? Guitar player from Kansas City. One of the greatest. Played trombone with Lunceford and he also played guitar. He played more guitar than anybody at that time. Can’t think of his name [Eddie Durham]. He died a few years ago. He was a bitch. He should have played guitar all the time, but he wanted to play trombone. He played trombone because he was a arranger, and he…
Who . . . when that sound was coming along, who set the standards for that? Who were some, one of the earliest guitar players to play like that?

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: I saw Banjo Bernie come through... And I found all them other virtuosos, Banjo Bernie and all them kind of people who played

ctx.x: I found when I got to New York... I looked around and saw all the virtuoso guitar players (there wasn't many [?] banjo players, and they weren't doing much. They were with tramp bands, or they were working in dives and... I saw Banjo Bernie come through, and I saw Speed, Speedy... Speedy worked with Luckey Roberts and them. And I looked in the big bands, and in Charlie Johnson's band was Bobby Johnson, who was neat, cool, clean, didn't have too much to say, tended to business -- a banjo player. There was guys…
There was [John] Truehart in Chick Webb's band, who was the master and the boss of rhythm. Everybody remarked how great he was.
